topic: The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere
subject: chemistry

items.q: For about how long have the proportions of the different gases in the atmosphere been much the same as they are today?
items.correct: Around 200 million years
items.misconception: About 4.6 billion years
items.why: 4.6 billion years is the one date students remember from this topic, so it is attached to any question about how long something has been true. 4.6 billion years is the age of the Earth. The atmosphere has only been like today's for the last 200 million years, a small fraction of that.
items.random_wrong: Some 2.7 billion years

items.q: Which gas makes up about four-fifths of today's atmosphere?
items.correct: Nitrogen, a very unreactive gas
items.misconception: Oxygen, the gas used in breathing
items.why: Oxygen is the gas students hear about constantly, in breathing, burning and rusting, so its importance is mistaken for its abundance. Nitrogen is rarely mentioned because it is unreactive. Importance is not abundance. Nitrogen is about 80% of the air and oxygen about 20%; oxygen matters because of what it does, not because there is a lot of it.
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide, made in fires

items.q: About what proportion of today's atmosphere is oxygen?
items.correct: About one-fifth, roughly 20%
items.misconception: About four-fifths, roughly 80%
items.why: Oxygen is the gas students hear about constantly, in breathing, burning and rusting, so its importance is mistaken for its abundance. Nitrogen is rarely mentioned because it is unreactive. Importance is not abundance. Nitrogen is about 80% of the air and oxygen about 20%; oxygen matters because of what it does, not because there is a lot of it.
items.random_wrong: About half of it, roughly 50%

items.q: Which of these is present in today's atmosphere only in a small proportion?
items.correct: Argon, one of the noble gases
items.misconception: Nitrogen, which came from volcanoes
items.why: Oxygen is the gas students hear about constantly, in breathing, burning and rusting, so its importance is mistaken for its abundance. Nitrogen is rarely mentioned because it is unreactive. Importance is not abundance. Nitrogen is about 80% of the air and oxygen about 20%; oxygen matters because of what it does, not because there is a lot of it.
items.random_wrong: Water vapour, which forms clouds

items.q: Why is the evidence about the Earth's early atmosphere limited?
items.correct: The time scale of 4.6 billion years has destroyed most of the record
items.misconception: Nobody was present at the time to observe what was happening
items.why: Students reach for a human explanation. 'Nobody was watching' feels like a reason, and it hides the real point about how much evidence survives 4.6 billion years. Scientists routinely study things nobody watched. The problem is the time scale: over 4.6 billion years the rocks that held the record have largely been destroyed or altered.
items.random_wrong: Gases cannot be detected or measured in rock samples at all

items.q: Theories about the Earth's early atmosphere have changed and developed over time. What does this best show?
items.correct: Theories are revised when new evidence becomes available
items.misconception: The scientists who worked earlier must have been careless
items.why: Everyday use of 'theory' as a guess, plus the idea that science delivers final answers, makes change look like failure rather than progress. Changing in the light of evidence is a strength, not a fault. Theories about the early atmosphere have developed as evidence has accumulated, and they may develop again.
items.random_wrong: A theory that has changed cannot really be trusted now

items.q: According to the theory in the specification, what released the gases that formed the early atmosphere?
items.correct: Intense volcanic activity in the first billion years
items.misconception: Photosynthesis carried out by the first algae and plants
items.why: Volcanoes are credited with making the early atmosphere, so students extend that credit to every gas, including oxygen. Volcanic gases contained little or no oxygen. The oxygen now in the atmosphere was produced by algae and plants through photosynthesis.
items.random_wrong: Gases brought to the Earth by comets and by meteorites

items.q: How does this theory explain the formation of the oceans?
items.correct: Volcanic water vapour condensed as the Earth cooled
items.misconception: Ice delivered by comets melted on the young Earth surface
items.why: Comet delivery appears in documentaries and sounds dramatic, so it displaces the volcanic outgassing the specification actually describes. The specification's theory is that volcanoes released water vapour along with the other gases, and that this vapour condensed to form the oceans.
items.random_wrong: Water vapour condensed because the young Earth heated up

items.q: The early atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today. What does that suggest it contained?
items.correct: Mainly carbon dioxide, with little or no oxygen gas present
items.misconception: Mainly oxygen, with only small traces of carbon dioxide
items.why: It is hard to picture an Earth without breathable air, so students carry today's composition backwards in time. Oxygen had to be made. Before photosynthesis the atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen, like Mars and Venus today.
items.random_wrong: About 80% nitrogen and about 20% oxygen, just as now

items.q: Where did the nitrogen in the atmosphere come from, according to this theory?
items.correct: Volcanoes produced it and it built up gradually
items.misconception: Plants released it during photosynthesis, like oxygen
items.why: Photosynthesis is the one gas-making process students know well, so it gets used to explain the origin of any atmospheric gas. Photosynthesis releases oxygen, not nitrogen. The specification says volcanoes produced the nitrogen, which built up gradually.
items.random_wrong: It was left over when carbon dioxide dissolved

items.q: Which two gases may have been present in small proportions in the early atmosphere?
items.correct: Methane and ammonia were possibly present
items.misconception: Methane and oxygen were quite possibly there
items.why: Once students learn that volcanoes made the early atmosphere, they assume the whole of today's air came the same way, oxygen included. The oxygen came later, from photosynthesis by algae and plants. Volcanic gases were mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour, with nitrogen building up gradually.
items.random_wrong: Ammonia and chlorine were possibly present

items.q: What happened to much of the carbon dioxide once the oceans had formed?
items.correct: It dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated
items.misconception: It was all used up by the algae during photosynthesis instead
items.why: Photosynthesis is taught first and taught hard, so it crowds out the ocean route, which is easy to overlook because it is not a biological process. Both matter. Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and was precipitated as carbonate sediments, and algae and plants also decreased it by photosynthesis.
items.random_wrong: It escaped into space while the surface of the Earth cooled

items.q: What effect did carbon dioxide dissolving in the new oceans have on the atmosphere?
items.correct: The amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere was reduced
items.misconception: The carbonates dissolved once more and released the gas
items.why: 'Dissolved' and 'precipitated' are easily swapped, and students expect a gas that dissolves to come back out again. Precipitation is the opposite of dissolving: an insoluble carbonate formed as a solid and settled as sediment, so the carbon stayed out of the atmosphere.
items.random_wrong: The amount of oxygen in the atmosphere fell sharply

items.q: Rocks about 3 billion years old contain iron minerals that only form when no oxygen is present. Which conclusion does this evidence best support?
items.correct: The atmosphere then contained little or no oxygen gas
items.misconception: The atmosphere then was mainly oxygen and nitrogen gas
items.why: It is hard to picture an Earth without breathable air, so students carry today's composition backwards in time. Oxygen had to be made. Before photosynthesis the atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen, like Mars and Venus today.
items.random_wrong: It proves the volcanic theory completely and finally

items.q: A student is given two different accounts of the Earth's early atmosphere and asked to evaluate them. What is the best approach?
items.correct: Judge how well each one fits the available evidence
items.misconception: Accept whichever of the accounts was published first
items.why: Everyday use of 'theory' as a guess, plus the idea that science delivers final answers, makes change look like failure rather than progress. Changing in the light of evidence is a strength, not a fault. Theories about the early atmosphere have developed as evidence has accumulated, and they may develop again.
items.random_wrong: Accept whichever account is written in the more detail

items.q: Which word equation represents the photosynthesis that produced the oxygen now in the atmosphere?
items.correct: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen
items.misconception: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water vapour
items.why: Photosynthesis and respiration use the same four substances, so a student who has learnt the substances but not the direction writes the equation backwards. Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and makes glucose and oxygen. The reverse equation is respiration.
items.random_wrong: oxygen + water -> glucose + carbon dioxide gas

items.q: Which balanced symbol equation represents photosynthesis?
items.why: Students add coefficients until the side they are looking at works out, then stop, without checking the other side. Balancing is a check across the arrow. Count each element on both sides: 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on the left, and the same on the right.
items.random_wrong: CO2 + H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2

items.q: When did algae first produce oxygen?
items.correct: About 2.7 billion years ago
items.misconception: Roughly 200 million years ago
items.why: 4.6 billion years is the one date students remember from this topic, so it is attached to any question about how long something has been true. 4.6 billion years is the age of the Earth. The atmosphere has only been like today's for the last 200 million years, a small fraction of that.
items.random_wrong: Some 4.6 billion years ago

items.q: Why were animals able to evolve long after algae first appeared?
items.correct: The percentage of oxygen increased gradually
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide rose to the level animals needed
items.why: Photosynthesis is taught first and taught hard, so it crowds out the ocean route, which is easy to overlook because it is not a biological process. Both matter. Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and was precipitated as carbonate sediments, and algae and plants also decreased it by photosynthesis.
items.random_wrong: Oxygen reached today's level as soon as algae did

items.q: How did algae and plants change the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
items.correct: They decreased it, as photosynthesis uses it up
items.misconception: They increased it, as photosynthesis produces it
items.why: Photosynthesis and respiration use the same four substances, so a student who has learnt the substances but not the direction writes the equation backwards. Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and makes glucose and oxygen. The reverse equation is respiration.
items.random_wrong: They had no effect, as they only ever produce oxygen

items.q: Apart from photosynthesis, what else decreased the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
items.correct: The formation of sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels holding carbon
items.misconception: The burning of the fossil fuels that contain carbon in them
items.why: Everything students hear about fossil fuels concerns burning them, so formation and combustion get merged into one idea. Burning releases the carbon; forming locked it away. As sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels formed, carbon dioxide in the atmosphere decreased.
items.random_wrong: The weathering of volcanic rock to give off nitrogen gas

items.q: Which sequence describes the main changes in the Earth's atmosphere over time?
items.correct: Mainly carbon dioxide, then oxygen rising as carbon dioxide fell
items.misconception: Mainly oxygen at first, then carbon dioxide rising steadily to today
items.why: It is hard to picture an Earth without breathable air, so students carry today's composition backwards in time. Oxygen had to be made. Before photosynthesis the atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen, like Mars and Venus today.
items.random_wrong: Mainly nitrogen at first, then volcanoes added the oxygen

items.q: How were deposits of limestone formed?
items.correct: From shells and skeletons deposited on the sea bed
items.misconception: From thick layers of plant material buried in swamps
items.why: Both are sedimentary and both store carbon, so the two origins get swapped when they are recalled together. Limestone is carbonate from marine shells and skeletons. Coal is compressed plant material from swamps.
items.random_wrong: From plankton buried in mud and heated under pressure

items.q: How did deposits of crude oil and natural gas form?
items.correct: From plankton buried in mud on the sea bed
items.misconception: From trees and ferns buried in ancient swamps on land
items.why: Coal is taught first and its plant origin is vivid, so the same story is reused for the other two fossil fuels. Coal came from land plants; crude oil and natural gas came from plankton, tiny marine organisms buried in mud on the sea bed.
items.random_wrong: From the shells of sea creatures on the sea bed

items.q: Roughly what percentage of the air is carbon dioxide?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide is one of the small proportions of various other gases, well under 1% of the atmosphere.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is a large fraction of the air, comparable with oxygen.
items.why: Carbon dioxide dominates lessons on climate change and on the early atmosphere, so students assume the amount present must be large. Carbon dioxide has a large effect for a very small amount. It sits in the 'small proportions of various other gases' along with water vapour and the noble gases.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are noble gases present in today's atmosphere?
items.correct: Yes. Noble gases, mainly argon, are among the small proportions of other gases in the atmosphere.
items.misconception: Noble gases are not in the air because they are unreactive.
items.why: Students meet the noble gases as a Group 0 curiosity and never connect them with air; 'unreactive' is heard as 'not found anywhere ordinary'. Unreactive does not mean absent. Argon is the third most abundant gas in dry air, and the noble gases are named in the specification as part of the atmosphere.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is water vapour part of the atmosphere?
items.correct: Yes, water vapour is one of the small proportions of various other gases in the atmosphere.
items.misconception: Water vapour makes up a large share of the air, or else it does not count as a gas of the atmosphere at all.
items.why: Water is met as a liquid, so students either leave it out of a list of atmospheric gases or, having seen clouds, assume there is a great deal of it. Water vapour is a gas and is named in the specification, but like carbon dioxide and the noble gases it is present only in a small proportion.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happened about 2.7 billion years ago?
items.correct: Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago, and soon after this oxygen appeared in the atmosphere.
items.misconception: 2.7 billion years ago is when the Earth formed, or when the atmosphere reached today's composition.
items.why: Several large numbers appear in this topic (4.6 billion, 2.7 billion, 200 million) and students attach them to the wrong events. 4.6 billion years is the age of the Earth, 2.7 billion years ago is when algae first produced oxygen, and 200 million years is how long the composition has been like today's.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Were methane and ammonia the main gases of the early atmosphere?
items.correct: No. There may have been small proportions of methane and ammonia; the early atmosphere was mainly carbon dioxide.
items.misconception: Methane and ammonia were the main components of the early atmosphere.
items.why: These two gases are memorable because they are unusual, so they get promoted from a footnote to the headline. The specification says the early atmosphere consisted mainly of carbon dioxide, and that there may have been small proportions of methane and ammonia.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the symbol equation for photosynthesis need balancing?
items.correct: Yes: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2, with the atoms of each element equal on both sides.
items.misconception: The formulae are what matter; the numbers in front can be left off or guessed.
items.why: Students treat an equation as a list of substances rather than a statement about numbers of atoms, so coefficients feel optional. Atoms are conserved. Glucose contains six carbon atoms, so six carbon dioxide molecules are needed, and the balanced equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which produced oxygen first, algae or plants?
items.correct: Algae first produced oxygen about 2.7 billion years ago; plants evolved over the next billion years.
items.misconception: Plants came first and algae appeared later.
items.why: Plants are the familiar photosynthesisers, so they are assumed to be the original ones; algae seem like a minor special case. Algae came first, about 2.7 billion years ago. Plants evolved over the following billion years and the percentage of oxygen went on rising.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the atmospheres of Mars and Venus like today?
items.correct: They consist of mainly carbon dioxide, which is why they are used as a model for the Earth's early atmosphere.
items.misconception: Mars and Venus have atmospheres like the Earth's today, with nitrogen and oxygen.
items.why: Planets are pictured as broadly similar worlds, and the comparison in the specification is read as 'they are like Earth' rather than 'Earth was once like them'. Their atmospheres are mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen, which is what the Earth's early atmosphere is thought to have been like.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What can evidence do for a theory about the early atmosphere?
items.correct: Evidence can support a theory or count against it, but with a 4.6 billion year time scale it rarely settles the matter.
items.misconception: One piece of evidence proves a theory, and the fuller account is always the better one.
items.why: School science is often presented as a set of confirmed results, so students expect proof rather than the weighing of competing explanations. Evaluation means judging how well each theory accounts for the available evidence, and saying how confident that evidence allows you to be.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How did the percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere change?
items.correct: It increased gradually over about a billion years, to a level that enabled animals to evolve.
items.misconception: Oxygen jumped straight to today's level as soon as algae appeared.
items.why: The single date of 2.7 billion years ago is remembered as the moment the modern atmosphere arrived, so the slow rise is lost. Oxygen appeared in the atmosphere soon after algae evolved, but the percentage rose gradually over the next billion years.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why did the water vapour from volcanoes condense?
items.correct: Because the Earth cooled, so the vapour turned to liquid water and formed the oceans.
items.misconception: The water vapour condensed because the Earth was heating up.
items.why: Condensation is associated with the presence of water rather than with a fall in temperature, and 'the early Earth was hot' is remembered without the cooling that followed. Condensation needs cooling. As the Earth cooled, the water vapour released by volcanoes condensed to form the oceans.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the products of photosynthesis in the specification equation?
items.correct: Glucose and oxygen.
items.misconception: The products are starch and oxygen.
items.why: Plants are known for storing starch, and the oxygen is the memorable product, so glucose gets displaced by starch. The specification gives carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen. Starch is made later from glucose and is not in this equation.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the reactants in photosynthesis?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide and water.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide alone, because light and chlorophyll do the rest.
items.why: Light is emphasised so heavily as the requirement for photosynthesis that water is forgotten as a reactant. Light is a condition, not a reactant. The reactants are carbon dioxide and water, which is why 6H2O appears in the balanced equation.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happened to the amount of carbon dioxide as the oceans formed?
items.correct: It decreased, because carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated as sediments.
items.misconception: The oceans made no difference to the atmosphere, or it was the oxygen that fell instead.
items.why: Students see dissolving as a change to the water rather than a removal from the air, so the atmospheric consequence is missed. Gas that dissolves has left the atmosphere. As carbonates precipitated, the carbon stayed in the sediments and atmospheric carbon dioxide fell.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.9.1 The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere
